fix.cost: The limit is per temporary table per connection; size it with your connection count in mind.
fix.sql:
SET GLOBAL tmp_table_size = 67108864;
SET GLOBAL max_heap_table_size = 67108864;
fix.summary: Check whether an index matching the GROUP BY or ORDER BY reduces temporary-table work (an ORDER BY that differs from the grouping can still need a temporary table and sort), or raise the in-memory limit to 64.0 MB (both variables: the smaller one wins). Set tmp_table_size to 67108864 now, and in the server's option file (my.cnf) so it survives a restart. Set max_heap_table_size to 67108864 now, and in the server's option file (my.cnf) so it survives a restart. Global values apply to new connections: reopen the application's existing connections, or have the application set these session variables on them.

findings.summary: The associated statements used 50.0 s of database time over the 1 minute since statistics were reset (89%). The temporary table behind a GROUP BY, DISTINCT or ORDER BY in this statement outgrows the in-memory limit (16.0 MB, the smaller of tmp_table_size and max_heap_table_size) and moves to disk, which is many times slower: 20 on-disk tables in 20 runs. Latest activity: 60 runs observed over 16 minutes of Culprit's scans on Oct 11, 15:49–16:05 UTC. This count is shown without extrapolating a daily rate.

caveats: Some high-frequency single-row lookups are legitimate (for example, by primary key on a hot path). Check the calling code before batching.

fix.summary: Reuse a result the application already has, or cache it for as long as it remains valid; access checks must still reflect permission changes. If the caller loops over items, load their rows in one query (WHERE key IN (…) or a join) before the loop; ORMs usually have an eager-loading option for this.

fix.summary: Touch tables and rows in the same order everywhere: Make every code path that changes shop.customers and shop.orders do it in one order (for example, always the parent row first, and rows sorted by key). Then the second transaction waits instead of deadlocking.

findings.summary: Two transactions locked shop.customers and shop.orders in opposite order and waited on each other; session 202's transaction was rolled back. With the same order in both, the second would simply wait instead of deadlocking.

items.detail: The rows don't arrive in the order the GROUP BY / DISTINCT needs, so MariaDB builds a temporary table (on disk once it outgrows tmp_table_size) and sorts the result.
items.fix: An index whose leading columns match the GROUP BY may let MariaDB group in index order and reduce grouping work. An ORDER BY that differs from the grouping, especially an aggregate such as COUNT(*) DESC, can still need a temporary table and sort. Filter rows before grouping, or keep a pre-aggregated result, to reduce that work.
items.title: Groups 500K rows in an internal temporary table, then sorts them (filesort)
items.verify: Explain again: look for grouping in index order or fewer rows entering the temporary table. A temporary table and sort for a different ORDER BY can remain; compare on-disk temporary tables on new runs to check the spill itself.
